summary: This bill makes states and local governments ineligible for Byrne or COPS federal law enforcement grants unless they certify that they do not charge the public any fees to view or obtain copies of body camera, dash camera, jail surveillance, or other law enforcement footage.

scores.thoughts: The bill conditions eligibility for existing Byrne and COPS grant programs on a certification regarding footage access fees. It neither increases nor decreases overall federal spending levels or appropriates new funds; it merely adds a programmatic requirement to already-authorized grants. No direct bearing on government spending.
The legislation contains no provisions related to tax rates, tax policy, revenue collection, or tax expenditures.
No provisions address healthcare delivery, insurance, public coverage, or market-based reforms.
No provisions address firearms regulation, permitting, or Second Amendment issues.
No provisions address immigration pathways, border enforcement, or immigrant protections.
No provisions address reproductive health services or abortion access.
No provisions address military budgets, defense programs, or national security spending.
No provisions address environmental regulations, climate policy, or conservation.
No provisions address welfare programs, food assistance, or other safety-net benefits.
No provisions address schools, school choice, or federal education policy.
No provisions address drug enforcement, decriminalization, or substance regulation.

The bill requires states and localities receiving Byrne or COPS grants to provide free public access to body-camera, dash-camera, and related law-enforcement footage. This directly advances police transparency and accountability, core elements of criminal-justice reform efforts. The magnitude is moderate because the change is limited to grant conditions rather than a broad statutory mandate.
No provisions address tariffs, trade agreements, or globalization.
No provisions address deficits, debt reduction, or fiscal policy.
No provisions address legal protections or rights for LGBTQ+ individuals.
No provisions address foreign assistance or international aid.
No provisions address voting access, election administration, or voter-ID requirements.

While the bill concerns access to law-enforcement video data, it regulates only government agencies receiving federal grants and does not impose new rules on private technology companies or general data-privacy standards. The connection is therefore tangential.
No provisions address worker protections, collective bargaining, or union rights.
No provisions address religious exemptions or anti-discrimination protections.
